paper_title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts 1. Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is typically carried out one domain at time, since each domain comes with its own data, verifier, and environment. common recipe is therefore to train domain experts separately from shared base model and then consolidate them into single model (Wang et al., 2026b, Ma et al., 2026a). Because new domains and stronger experts keep arriving, this consolidation is not one-time step but continual process. Ideally, each new expert would be absorbed like an installed module, such that (i) the model gains what the expert learned in its domain, (ii) everything the model could already do, in the other experts domains and in general, is left intact, and (iii) the cost of the update depends only on the new expert, not on how many experts came before. Existing approaches fall into two groups. The first consolidates all experts into single set of weights. Joint multi-task RL must rerun RL on every domain whenever one is added. Sequential RL (Wang et al., 2026a) trains only on the new domain, but earlier gains are susceptible to irreversible damage from later stages. Weight merging (Ilharco et al., 2023, Yadav et al., 2023) combines experts by parameter arithmetic, where their updates can interfere. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) (Wang et al., 2026b, Ma et al., 2026a) must retrain the student against all teachers. All four also apply one fixed mixture to every request and overwrite the base weights, which can degrade performance outside the target domains (Wang et al., 2026c). The second group keeps experts separate and selects them per request. Expert routing depends on router that is hard to train and must be updated whenever an expert is added, cannot combine experts within request, and must host full model per expert. Merging LoRA experts per request (Huang et al., 2023, Prabhakar et al., 2024) avoids these issues but adds adapter computation to every layer at every decoding step. Both groups keep experts in model parameters. We instead make each expert part of the models input, and propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD) (Figure 2). During training, CSPD keeps the pre-RL model frozen and distills each post-RL expert into its own soft prompt (Lester et al., 2021) of 256 vectors, using only that experts verifier-filtered responses (Kim and Rush, 2016). Each soft prompt is trained independently. To prepare the prompts for later combination, half of the training examples place random context prefix before the prompt, so that it works regardless of what precedes it. At inference, the prompts are composed directly by concatenating them in the system message, without any joint training. Adding an expert therefore requires training only its prompt, removing an expert requires only dropping its prompt, and the backbone is never modified. Unlike merged or routed LoRA experts, the prompts are plug-in modules, with no merging coefficient or router to refit when the set of experts changes. Merging experts in input space proves surprisingly effective. single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert. Across 23 math, code, and agent settings, it recovers at least 90% of the teachers improvement over the pre-RL model in 22 of them, and matches or exceeds the teacher in 15. Independently trained prompts exhibit strong composability. In multi-expert setting (Wang et al., 2026b), we distill soft prompts from experts in instruction following, science, code, and math, and add them to the frozen student one at time, as in continual post-training. The four-domain average rises with every addition, from 50.41 to 67.83, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.79) without any joint training. The composition generalizes best beyond the training domains. Among the compared methods, it attains the highest mean score across six held-out benchmarks (56.6, versus 53.5 for MOPD). soft prompt learns behavior rather than words. On GPT-OSS math expert, the prompt closes 86.8% of the teacherstudent KL gap, mainly by making the student check its intermediate results, while written instructions with the same intent close at most 2.1% (Section 4). Experiments We first evaluate whether soft prompt can recover single RL expert (Section 3.2). We then evaluate the composition of independently distilled prompts in-domain (Section 3.3) and in continual post-training setting (Section 3.4), and evaluate out-of-domain generalization (Section 3.5). Finally, we measure the cost of serving distinct prompt per request (Section 3.6). 3.1. Evaluation Metrics We report absolute task scores and the fraction of the RL teachers performance gain recovered by the prompted student. Let AS, AT, and AS+P denote the student, teacher, and prompted-student scores, each either single-task score or an average over multiple tasks. For AT > AS, recovery is = AS+P AS AT AS 100%. The table also gives model links and references, and evaluation details are in Appendices B.3 and B.1. The 23 settings are deliberately diverse. They span math reasoning, code generation on LiveCodeBench, and multi-step agent tasks on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1. The models range from 7B to 35B parameters and include both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures from many model families, and their teachers were trained with different RL recipes and data. Coefficient sweeps and baseline training settings are in Appendix D. 6 Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts Concatenated prompts recover the combined expert gain. Table 2 reports the single-domain and composition results. Composing the four prompts raises the students average score from 50.41 to 67.83, recovering approximately 107.5% of the aggregate expert gain and exceeding the average of the individual experts (66.61), which corresponds to an oracle router that sends each benchmark to its own domain expert. The same prompts evaluated individually average 65.38. Composition raises GPQA-Diamond from 49.24 to 57.77 and IFBench from 66.71 to 68.42, while AIME24 decreases slightly from 80.89 to 80.47. The reverse order ISCM gives similar average of 67.72. Independently learned modules can therefore contribute beyond their own training domains, although composition does not improve every domain uniformly. Training with varied context helps composition. Each prompt is trained alone but used after other prompts at inference. Prefix-robust training (Section 2.2) exposes it to varied preceding text during training. This makes the composition more stable (Table 2 and Appendix C). Input-space composition matches weight-space consolidation. CSPD achieves an average score on par with MOPD (67.79) and higher than expert TIES (67.47) and expert TA (67.27). It also exceeds LoRA distillation followed by TA (65.50) or TIES (66.19), where the LoRA adapters use the same distillation data as the soft prompts. Performance varies by domain. CSPD scores higher than MOPD on GPQA-Diamond and IFBench, while MOPD performs better on AIME24 and LiveCodeBench. Thus, composing in input space reaches the in-domain performance of consolidating in weight space, while every expert remains separate module that was trained without access to the others. 3.4. Adding and Removing Experts We next evaluate adding experts one at time, using the four prompts from Section 3.3, keeping the backbone and all prompts fixed throughout. Continual addition. Starting from the unprompted student, experts arrive in the order instruction following (I), science (S), code (C), and math (M). Each new prompt is placed before the existing ones, yielding the inputs Student SI CSI MCSI, where the leftmost module is the most recent. The final input is the default composition of Table 2. We evaluate all four domains after each addition. The average rises from the students 50.41 to 60.99, 61.67, 63.67, and 67.83 (Figure 3a), ending above the average of the individual experts (66.61), without retraining any existing module. Individual domains exhibit both positive and negative interactions. Adding code reduces IFBench from 66.71 to 64.58, while subsequently adding math raises it to 68.42. Appending each new prompt instead gives similar trajectory (Appendix C). Module removal and cross-domain contributions. Comparison with progressive training and merging. natural alternative is to train each new prompt in the context of the earlier ones, as in Progressive Prompts (Razdaibiedina et al., 2023), where each new prompt is trained with all previous prompts frozen in front of it, so it can adapt to the existing composition. Because progressive training places each new prompt in front of the previous ones, we compare it with independent prompts in the same prepended order (I, SI, CSI, MCSI), with the same optimizer and number of updates. Both start from the same prompt. Independent training gives higher average at every stage (Figure 4): 61.67 versus 56.44 after S, 63.67 versus 58.28 after C, and 67.83 versus 65.17 after M. Progressive training also erodes the earliest capability, reducing IFBench to 52.71, 50.88, and 61.42 at these stages. Fitting new module to particular composition therefore does not help later joint use, and freezing earlier prompts alone does not preserve their behavior. Independent training is therefore both simpler and more effective in this setting. Adding capabilities through the input, with the backbone frozen, thus largely preserves the students general capabilities. 3.6. Serving Efficiency soft prompt adds parameters only at the input. It is processed once during prefill, and every later decoding step only attends to its cached keys and values, so relative to the backbone the only cost is slightly longer context (Appendix F). LoRA adapter, by contrast, adds computation to every layer at every decoding step. Because every expert is an input to the same frozen model, requests that use different experts, or different combinations of them, can also share one batch. We measure the cost of this by assigning distinct adapter to every request, the extreme case of per-user personalization, and comparing throughput and first-token latency against the same backbone served without adapters. Experimental setting. We serve GPT-OSS-20B in BF16 on single NVIDIA B200 with SGLang. We compare the unadapted backbone, 256-vector soft prompts, and unmerged rank-4 LoRA adapters served with the CSGMV backend. Each request has 20,480 text input tokens and generates 512 tokens, simulating an agent setting. SP adds 256 vectors to the input. We use matched text inputs across configurations and register the synthetic adapters before timing generation. We vary the concurrency limit over 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32. After warm-up burst of requests, closedloop client issues 8C measured requests, starting new one whenever slot becomes available. All three configurations use the same KV-cache budget at each concurrency level, with 524,288 tokens through = 16 and 1,048,576 at = 24 and 32. We report aggregate output tokens per second from the first request submission to the last completion, and the 95th percentile of the time from request submission to receipt of the first token. Multi-adapter serving. SP throughput stays within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone across the seven concurrency levels (Figure 5). Relative to LoRA, the advantage is largest with one request in flight, where SP delivers 4.12 the output throughput of LoRA. At 32 concurrent requests, SP serves 715.4 output tokens/s, compared with 721.3 for the backbone and 298.5 for LoRA. At this operating point, SP delivers 2.40 the throughput of LoRA and reduces P95 time to first token from 39.21 to 17.26 seconds, 2.27 reduction, close to the backbones 16.89 seconds. Speculative decoding. Soft prompts also remain compatible with draft models trained on the backbone. Adding 256-vector prompt reduces the average acceptance length from 2.34 to 2.28 for EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) (2.6%) and from 2.96 to 2.82 for DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) (4.7%). Acceptance length does not directly measure end-to-end latency. 10 Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts Figure 5. Request-specific adapter serving on one B200. Higher throughput (left) and lower P95 time to first token (right) are better. At 32 concurrent requests, the arrows show the SP-to-LoRA throughput ratio and the LoRA-to-SP latency ratio. The lower panels show SPs percentage change relative to the unadapted backbone, with zero indicating equal performance. 4. What Does Soft Prompt Learn? We analyze one expert from Table 1, the 256-vector soft prompt that distills GPT-OSS-Swallow-20B-RL into GPT-OSS-Swallow-20B-SFT for math. The teacher, the student, and the prompted student answer 100 held-out AIME and MATH-500 questions. Each model then reads the same answers, and at every response position we compare its next-token distribution with the teachers. See Appendix for details. The nearest word of soft prompt vector does not tell what the vector learned. Across six models, 84100% of the vectors keep their initialization token as the nearest word, even though in five of them the vectors move far from that token (median cosine similarity 0.250.34). The soft prompt moves the student most of the way to the teacher, mainly by making it check its intermediate results. It closes 86.8% of the teacherstudent KL gap. The tokens it raises most are ?, But, and Check, and those it lowers most are paragraph breaks, So, and Thus (Figure 6b). Instead of stating result and moving on, the prompted student first questions or checks it, as the teacher does. Written instructions with the same intent do not reproduce the effect. Instructions asking the model to check and verify its work close at most 2.1% of the gap, and raising the reasoning effort closes none (Figure 6a). The soft prompt acts mainly through response tokens attending to it directly, rather than by changing how the model reads the question. When only response tokens may attend to the soft prompt, 80% of its improvement remains, but only 33% remains when only input tokens may attend to it (Figure 6c). Taken together, soft prompt does not learn message that can be put into words. It learns the teachers 11 Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts reasoning behavior, here checking intermediate results, and applies it through the attention of the response tokens. Figure 6. What the GPT-OSS math soft prompt does. (a) Share of the teacherstudent KL gap closed by the soft prompt, written instructions, and high reasoning effort. (b) Tokens that appear most often among the 2,000 positions where the soft prompt raises (blue) or lowers (red) the probability of the trace token the most. marks leading space. (c) Share of the soft prompts improvement kept when only some tokens may attend to it. Details in Appendix G. 5. Discussion Why compose in input space? Weight-space consolidation writes every expert into the same parameters, so adding an expert means re-consolidating the model, and the experts can interfere with one another and with the backbones general capabilities. CSPD separates acquiring capability from combining capabilities. Each prompt is distilled using only its own teacher and data, prompts meet only at inference, and the backbone never changes. This separation lets experts be trained in parallel by different parties, added or replaced without revisiting earlier domains, and removed exactly by dropping their prompt. Our results show that this separation does not cost in-domain performance relative to MOPD, and that it better preserves out-of-domain behavior. The progressive-training comparison further suggests that composition does not require each module to be trained with knowledge of the others. Plug-in experts versus multi-LoRA. Combining LoRA experts from different domains usually takes one of two forms. Merging adds their weight updates with tuned coefficients (Ilharco et al., 2023, Yadav et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2023, Prabhakar et al., 2024), so all experts write into the same weights and can interfere. With the same distillation data, merged LoRA adapters reach 65.50 with TA and 66.19 with TIES, below the 67.83 of composed soft prompts  (Table 2)  . Mixture-style methods instead learn router or gate over the adapters (Buehler and Buehler, 2024, Zadouri et al., 2024), which must be retrained whenever an expert is added. soft prompt is plug-in module. Adding an expert trains only its prompt, removing one drops its prompt exactly, and several experts act together within request by concatenation, with no coefficient or router to fit. Different requests in one batch can also use different sets of prompts on the same unchanged backbone, which gives 2.40 the output throughput of rank-4 LoRA with 32 distinct adapters (Section 3.6). 12 Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts Limitations. Our composition study uses one backbone, four domains, and single training seed. Whether composition continues to improve as the number of experts grows, and how it depends on the relations between domains, remain open. Experts do interact, both positively and negatively (Section 3.4). Several reported numbers, including single-expert checkpoints and TA coefficients, are selected on the evaluation benchmarks, and small teacher gains make some recovery ratios noisy, so we report absolute scores throughout (Appendix B.3). Each prompt adds 256 positions to the context, so attention and KV-cache costs grow with the number of composed experts. Finally, prompts are tied to their backbone and require RL teachers for supervision, so moving to new backbone requires re-distillation. Toward continual post-training. CSPD suggests different shape for post-training, with frozen backbone and growing library of compact expert modules, each distilled when new capability becomes available and composed as needed. Four directions follow. The first is scale, with more backbones, larger prompt libraries, several seeds, and more arrival orders. The second is prompt selection, learning which prompts each request needs instead of choosing them by hand. The third is mechanism, understanding why prompts transfer across domains and how several prompts share attention. The fourth is cost, with shorter prompts for large libraries and full training-cost comparison with MOPD and LoRA. 6. Related Work Capacity requirements of post-training. LoRA can match full fine-tuning in selected post-training regimes (Schulman and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Single-layer training, sparse subnetworks, and low-dimensional adapters can also recover substantial RL gains (Zhang et al., 2026, Mukherjee et al., 2025, Morris et al., 2026), while SGD-based RL exhibits sparse updates (Mukherjee et al., 2026). These findings motivate studying input-space representations of expert capabilities. Distilling post-training capabilities. Sequence-level distillation transfers teacher-generated responses, including reasoning capabilities (Kim and Rush, 2016, DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), whereas on-policy methods supervise student-generated trajectories (Agarwal et al., 2024, Gu et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2025, Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates several experts into one student (Wang et al., 2026b, Ma et al., 2026a). Approaching teacher performance in-domain can nevertheless accompany out-of-domain losses (Wang et al., 2026c), motivating evaluation beyond the distilled capabilities. Representations of adaptation. Adaptation can reside in weights, continuous inputs, layerwise prefixes, or hidden-state interventions (Hu et al., 2021, Lester et al., 2021, Li and Liang, 2021, Wu et al., 2024). PromptKD and soft-prompt teachers use learned prompts to guide distillation into student weights (Kim et al., 2024, Ma et al., 2026b). DDPT instead places demonstration-induced reasoning in dynamically selected prompts (Teng et al., 2026). Soft prompts can also receive distilled safety behavior (Alfarra et al., 2026). Cartridges train keyvalue cache prefixes to compress long contexts through self-study (Eyuboglu et al., 2025). Concurrent with our work, Hypertune trains keyvalue cache prefixes directly with RL or SFT, adding co-residence training so that several prefixes can be loaded together (Hyperstition, 2026). CSPD instead learns prompts in the input embedding space by distilling existing RL experts, trains each prompt in isolation, and composes them by concatenation. An input-space prompt can also be prefilled once into keyvalue prefix for serving. Composition, continual learning, and efficient serving. Model soups, Task Arithmetic, and interferenceaware merging combine weight updates (Wortsman et al., 2022, Ilharco et al., 2023, Yadav et al., 2023, Yu 13 Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts et al., 2024), with mixed results for RL experts (Wu et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026b). Adapter composition combines updates or learns gates (Pfeiffer et al., 2021, Huang et al., 2023, Prabhakar et al., 2024, Buehler and Buehler, 2024, Zadouri et al., 2024), while BAR composes experts through routed mixture-of-experts architecture (Morrison et al., 2026). In input space, APT learns composable prompts and ATTEMPT mixes source prompts (Bowman et al., 2023, Asai et al., 2022). Progressive Prompts freezes earlier prompts during continual learning (Razdaibiedina et al., 2023), and Skill Neologisms composes independently learned skill embeddings (Berthon et al., 2026). Deployment work optimizes concurrent adapters (Chen et al., 2023, Sheng et al., 2024), prefill-only adaptation (Lanpouthakoun et al., 2026), and speculative decoding (Li et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2026). CSPD connects these research directions by independently distilling RL experts into prompts on shared frozen backbone, then evaluating their concatenation, out-of-domain behavior, and serving efficiency. 7. Conclusion We presented CSPD, which distills each post-RL expert into an independently trained soft prompt on frozen pre-RL backbone and composes experts by concatenating their prompts. single prompt recovers at least 90% of the teachers gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Four prompts from different domains, trained without access to each other, compose to match MOPD in-domain, and the average rises with every expert added one at time, as in continual post-training. The composition also attains the highest mean score on held-out benchmarks among the compared methods. Because the experts live in the input, serving them costs little more than serving the backbone alone. These results suggest input-space modules as practical foundation for continual post-training.

sections.title: Impact Statement
sections.content: This work studies modular transfer of post-trained behavior. Compact, attachable modules may make specialized behaviors easier to distribute and serve, including behaviors that require safety evaluation. Freezing the backbone does not guarantee that an attached prompt, or combination of prompts, preserves safety properties, and our XSTest evaluation covers only refusal behavior on the tested requests. Release decisions should consider model and dataset terms, generated training material, and the behavior of the resulting modules alone and in combination.
